lessons.title: Atoms, Elements, Compounds and the Model of the Atom
lessons.description: How atoms are structured, how the atomic model developed, and how to work out electronic structure.
lessons.content_html:
Atoms, Elements and Compounds

All substances are made of atoms. An atom is the smallest part of an element that can exist. There are about 100 different types of atom, and each type is a different element. Elements are shown in the periodic table. Each element has its own chemical symbol — for example, O for oxygen, Na for sodium, and Fe for iron.

Key Fact

An element contains only one type of atom. A compound contains two or more different elements chemically bonded together. A mixture contains two or more substances that are not chemically bonded.

A compound is formed when atoms of two or more different elements are chemically bonded together. For example, water (H₂O) is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen. Carbon dioxide (CO₂) is a compound of carbon and oxygen. The properties of a compound are different from the properties of the elements it contains — for example, hydrogen and oxygen are both gases at room temperature, but water is a liquid.

Mixtures

A mixture consists of two or more elements or compounds not chemically combined together. The chemical properties of each substance in the mixture are unchanged. Mixtures can be separated by physical processes such as filtration, distillation, and chromatography — these do not involve chemical reactions, so no new substances are made.

Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid, for example sand from water. Simple distillation separates a solvent from a solution, for example water from salt water. Fractional distillation separates a mixture of liquids with different boiling points, such as crude oil. Chromatography separates dissolved substances based on how they move through a stationary phase — useful for identifying unknown substances such as food colourings.

The Structure of the Atom

Atoms consist of a small, dense nucleus surrounded by electrons. The nucleus contains two types of particle: protons (which carry a positive charge) and neutrons (which carry no charge). Electrons orbit the nucleus in energy levels (shells) and carry a negative charge.

Key Fact

In an atom, the number of protons always equals the number of electrons, so atoms have no overall electrical charge. The relative masses and charges are: proton (mass 1, charge +1), neutron (mass 1, charge 0), electron (mass very nearly 0, charge −1).

The radius of an atom is about 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. The radius of the nucleus is less than 1/10,000 of the radius of the atom. Most of the mass of an atom is concentrated in the nucleus, while most of the atom is empty space.

Atomic Number, Mass Number and Isotopes

The atomic number (also called the proton number) is the number of protons in the nucleus. It defines what element an atom is — all atoms of the same element have the same atomic number. The mass number is the total number of protons plus neutrons in the nucleus.

To find the number of neutrons: subtract the atomic number from the mass number. For example, sodium has an atomic number of 11 and a mass number of 23, so it has 23 − 11 = 12 neutrons.

Isotopes are atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. This gives them different mass numbers. For example, carbon-12 has 6 protons and 6 neutrons, while carbon-14 has 6 protons and 8 neutrons. Both are carbon because they have the same atomic number (6).

Because isotopes have different masses, the relative atomic mass (Aᵣ) of an element is an average value that takes into account the abundance of each isotope. It is calculated as a weighted mean: Aᵣ = Σ(isotope mass × abundance) ÷ Σ(abundance). The Aᵣ shown on the periodic table is not always a whole number because it is an average. For example, chlorine has two isotopes: chlorine-35 (75%) and chlorine-37 (25%), giving Aᵣ = (35 × 75 + 37 × 25) ÷ 100 = 35.5.

The Development of the Atomic Model

Our understanding of the atom has changed over time as new evidence became available. Before the discovery of the electron, atoms were thought to be tiny, solid, indivisible spheres — this was John Dalton’s model from the early 1800s.

1897

Discovery of the Electron

J.J. Thomson discovered that atoms contain smaller, negatively charged particles called electrons. He proposed the plum pudding model — a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it, like plums in a pudding.

1909

Alpha Scattering Experiment

Rutherford, Geiger and Marsden fired alpha particles at thin gold foil. Most passed straight through, but a small number were deflected at large angles and some bounced straight back. This could not be explained by the plum pudding model.

1911

The Nuclear Model

Rutherford concluded that the atom must have a small, dense, positively charged nucleus at its centre, with electrons orbiting around it. Most of the atom is empty space.

1913

Bohr’s Model

Niels Bohr adapted Rutherford’s model by suggesting that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances in fixed energy levels (shells), rather than orbiting randomly. Later experiments confirmed the existence of these energy levels.

1932

Discovery of the Neutron

James Chadwick discovered a neutral particle inside the nucleus — the neutron. This completed the modern model of the atom with protons, neutrons and electrons.

Key Fact

The alpha scattering experiment disproved the plum pudding model. Most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil (atom is mostly empty space), but some bounced back (nucleus is small, dense and positive).

Electronic Structure

Electrons occupy energy levels (shells) around the nucleus. The first shell (closest to the nucleus) holds a maximum of 2 electrons. The second and third shells each hold a maximum of 8 electrons. Electrons fill the lowest energy level first before moving to the next.

To work out the electronic structure of an atom, find the element on the periodic table and note its atomic number (the number of protons, which equals the number of electrons). Fill the first shell with up to 2 electrons, the second with up to 8, and the third with up to 8. For example: sodium has 11 electrons, so its electronic structure is 2, 8, 1. Chlorine has 17 electrons, so its electronic structure is 2, 8, 7. Calcium has 20 electrons: 2, 8, 8, 2.

The electronic structure of an atom determines its chemical properties. Elements in the same group of the periodic table have the same number of electrons in their outer shell, which is why they react in similar ways. The group number tells you how many outer-shell electrons an atom has (for Groups 1–7).
lessons.exam_tip_html: For “describe” questions about the development of the atomic model, make sure you name the scientist AND explain what their evidence showed — not just what their model looked like. For calculate questions on subatomic particles, always show your working: number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number. Examiners award marks for the method even if your final answer is wrong.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Atoms have a small, dense nucleus (protons + neutrons) surrounded by electrons in energy levels. The number of protons defines the element and equals the number of electrons in a neutral atom.
  • The atomic model evolved from Dalton’s solid sphere, through Thomson’s plum pudding model, to Rutherford’s nuclear model, Bohr’s energy levels, and Chadwick’s discovery of the neutron.
  • Electronic structures are written as numbers separated by commas (e.g. 2, 8, 1 for sodium) and determine an element’s chemical properties and position in the periodic table.

lessons.title: The Periodic Table and Its Groups
lessons.description: How the periodic table is organised, and the properties of Groups 0, 1, and 7.
lessons.content_html:
How the Periodic Table Is Organised

The periodic table arranges all known elements in order of increasing atomic number (the number of protons in the nucleus). Elements with similar chemical properties are placed in the same vertical column, called a group. The horizontal rows are called periods.

The group number tells you how many electrons an element has in its outer shell. For example, all Group 1 elements have one electron in their outer shell, all Group 7 elements have seven, and Group 0 elements have a full outer shell. This is why elements in the same group behave in similar ways — their chemical reactions depend on the arrangement of their outer electrons.

Key Fact

Elements in the same group have the same number of electrons in their outer shell. This is why they have similar chemical properties. The group number equals the number of outer-shell electrons (except Group 0, which has a full outer shell of 2 or 8 electrons).

Development of the Periodic Table

In the early 1800s, scientists tried to arrange the known elements by atomic mass. However, this produced tables where elements with very different properties ended up in the same group. The breakthrough came from the Russian chemist Mendeleev in 1869.

Mendeleev arranged the elements by atomic mass, but he did two things that made his table far more successful than earlier attempts. First, he left gaps where he believed undiscovered elements should fit. Second, he predicted the properties of these missing elements based on the trends he observed in surrounding elements.

When elements like germanium (which Mendeleev called “eka-silicon”) were later discovered, their properties closely matched his predictions. This confirmed the usefulness of his table and convinced other scientists it was correct. Mendeleev also swapped the order of some elements (e.g. tellurium and iodine) so that they sat in groups with elements that had similar properties, even though this meant they were not strictly in atomic mass order.

The modern periodic table is arranged by atomic number rather than atomic mass. This resolved the problems Mendeleev encountered when swapping element positions. Knowledge of electrons and their arrangement in shells (thanks to scientists like Niels Bohr) explained why elements in the same group have similar properties — they have the same number of outer-shell electrons.

Key Fact

Mendeleev left gaps in his periodic table for undiscovered elements and predicted their properties. When these elements were later found (e.g. germanium), his predictions were confirmed — proving the table’s validity.

Metals and Non-Metals

The periodic table is divided into metals (on the left and centre) and non-metals (on the right). Metals make up the majority of elements.

Metals typically have high melting and boiling points, are good conductors of heat and electricity, and are malleable (can be hammered into shape) and ductile (can be drawn into wires). When metals react, they lose electrons to form positive ions. Non-metals are typically poor conductors, have lower melting points, and are brittle when solid. When non-metals react, they gain electrons to form negative ions.

The transition metals sit in the central block of the periodic table, between Group 2 and Group 3. They include familiar metals like iron, copper, and gold. Compared to Group 1 metals, transition metals have higher melting points, higher densities, and are much stronger and harder.

Key properties of transition metals include: they can have variable oxidation states (charges), they often form coloured compounds (e.g. copper sulfate is blue), and they are useful as catalysts (e.g. iron in the Haber process). Roman numerals in compound names (such as copper(II) sulfate) indicate which oxidation state the transition metal is using.

Group 1 — The Alkali Metals

Group 1 elements are lithium (Li), sodium (Na), potassium (K), rubidium (Rb), caesium (Cs), and francium (Fr). They are called the alkali metals because they react with water to produce alkaline solutions (metal hydroxides).

All Group 1 metals have one electron in their outer shell, which they lose easily during reactions to form +1 ions. This makes them very reactive. They are soft enough to cut with a knife, have relatively low melting points for metals, and have low densities — lithium, sodium, and potassium all float on water.

When alkali metals react with water, they produce a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas:

\(lithium + water \rightarrow \text{lithium hydroxide} + hydrogen\)
\(sodium + water \rightarrow \text{sodium hydroxide} + hydrogen\)
\(potassium + water \rightarrow \text{potassium hydroxide} + hydrogen\)

The metal hydroxides formed are alkalis — this is why universal indicator turns purple when potassium reacts with water (KOH is strongly alkaline). Reactivity increases down the group because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more easily lost. Lithium fizzes gently, sodium fizzes vigorously and melts into a ball, and potassium reacts so violently that the hydrogen produced ignites with a lilac flame.

Key Fact — Group 1 Trends

Going down Group 1: reactivity increases, melting point decreases, and density generally increases. Reactivity increases because the outer electron is further from the nucleus, so it is lost more easily.

Group 7 — The Halogens

Group 7 elements are fluorine (F), chlorine (Cl), bromine (Br), iodine (I), and astatine (At). They are called the halogens. They exist as diatomic molecules (e.g. Cl₂, Br₂). All Group 7 elements have seven electrons in their outer shell and gain one electron during reactions to form \(- 1 ions\).

Going down the group, the halogens change state at room temperature: fluorine is a pale yellow gas, chlorine is a green gas, bromine is a red-brown liquid, and iodine is a grey solid that sublimes to a purple vapour. Melting and boiling points increase down the group because the molecules get larger, so the intermolecular forces between them become stronger.

A more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive halogen from an aqueous solution of its salt. For example:

\(chlorine + \text{sodium bromide} \rightarrow \text{sodium chloride} + bromine\)

Chlorine displaces bromine because chlorine is more reactive (it is higher in the group). Reactivity decreases down Group 7 because the outer shell is further from the nucleus, so the attraction for an incoming electron is weaker. There is also more electron shielding from inner electron shells.

Key Fact — Group 7 Trends

Going down Group 7: reactivity decreases, melting and boiling points increase. This is the opposite trend to Group 1. Reactivity decreases because the outer shell is further from the nucleus, so gaining an electron becomes harder.

Group 0 — The Noble Gases

Group 0 elements are helium (He), neon (Ne), argon (Ar), krypton (Kr), xenon (Xe), and radon (Rn). They are called the noble gases. They are unreactive (inert) because they have a full outer shell of electrons — helium has 2, and the others have 8. Since they do not need to gain, lose, or share electrons, they rarely form compounds.

Noble gases are colourless, odourless, and exist as monatomic (single atom) gases. Their boiling points are very low but increase down the group as the atoms get larger and intermolecular forces increase. Uses include: helium in balloons and airships (low density, non-flammable), neon in illuminated signs (glows red-orange), argon in filament lamps and welding (provides an inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation).

Chemical reactions involve the transfer or sharing of electrons in the outer shell. Noble gases already have a stable electron configuration (a full outer shell), so they have no tendency to react. This is the same electron arrangement that other elements try to achieve when they form ions or covalent bonds. Helium’s outer shell holds a maximum of 2 electrons (it only has one shell), while all other noble gases have 8 electrons in their outer shell.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions on Group 1 and Group 7 trends, always link the trend to electron structure. Saying “reactivity increases down Group 1” alone is not enough for full marks — you need to explain why (the outer electron is further from the nucleus, so it is more easily lost). For compare questions, make sure you state the trend for both groups and explain the reason for each, linking to whether electrons are lost or gained.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The periodic table is arranged by atomic number; elements in the same group have the same number of outer-shell electrons and similar chemical properties. Mendeleev’s key insight was leaving gaps and predicting undiscovered elements.
  • Group 1 (alkali metals) have 1 outer electron, react with water to form alkaline hydroxides, and get more reactive going down the group. Group 7 (halogens) have 7 outer electrons, gain 1 electron in reactions, and get less reactive going down. Group 0 (noble gases) have full outer shells and are unreactive.
  • Metals (left/centre) lose electrons to form positive ions; non-metals (right) gain electrons to form negative ions. Transition metals have high melting points, variable oxidation states, and form coloured compounds.

lessons.title: Ionic, Covalent and Metallic Bonding
lessons.description: How atoms bond by transferring or sharing electrons, and how metallic bonding holds metals together.
lessons.content_html:
Why Do Atoms Bond?

Atoms are most stable when they have a full outer shell of electrons. For most atoms, this means having eight electrons in their outer shell — a pattern sometimes called the octet rule. Noble gases already have full outer shells, which is why they are unreactive. All other atoms achieve stability by bonding with other atoms — either by transferring electrons or sharing them.

There are three main types of bonding you need to know for your GCSE: ionic bonding (transferring electrons), covalent bonding (sharing electrons), and metallic bonding (sharing delocalised electrons). Each type produces substances with very different properties.

Ionic Bonding

ionic bonding occurs between a metal and a non-metal. The metal atom transfers one or more electrons from its outer shell to the non-metal atom. This is not sharing — the electrons physically move from one atom to the other.

When a metal atom loses electrons, it becomes a positively charged ion (because it now has more protons than electrons). When a non-metal atom gains electrons, it becomes a negatively charged ion. The strong electrostatic attraction between these oppositely charged ions is what holds the compound together.

Key Fact

In ionic bonding, metals lose electrons to form positive ions, and non-metals gain electrons to form negative ions. The strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions hold the ionic compound together.

Sodium (Na) is in Group 1, so it has one electron in its outer shell. Chlorine (Cl) is in Group 7, so it has seven electrons in its outer shell and needs one more to be full. Sodium transfers its one outer electron to chlorine. Sodium becomes Na⁺ (a positive ion) and chlorine becomes Cl⁻ (a negative ion). The two ions attract each other strongly, forming sodium chloride.

Magnesium (Mg) is in Group 2, so it has two electrons in its outer shell. Oxygen (O) is in Group 6, so it has six electrons in its outer shell and needs two more. Magnesium transfers both of its outer electrons to oxygen. Magnesium becomes Mg²⁺ and oxygen becomes O²⁻. Notice that atoms with more electrons to lose or gain form ions with higher charges.

Dot and Cross Diagrams for Ionic Bonds

A dot and cross diagram shows which electrons belong to which atom. Electrons from one atom are drawn as dots and electrons from the other as crosses. In an ionic bond, the transferred electrons move completely into the receiving atom’s shell. The ions are shown in square brackets with the charge written as a superscript outside.

When drawing dot and cross diagrams for ionic compounds, remember: only show the outer shell electrons (this is what the exam expects), draw square brackets around each ion, and always include the ion charge. The exam may ask you to draw these for compounds like NaCl, MgO, or Na₂O.

Covalent Bonding

covalent bonding occurs between two non-metal atoms. Instead of transferring electrons, the atoms share pairs of electrons. Each shared pair of electrons forms one covalent bond. The atoms are held together because the shared electrons are attracted to the nuclei of both atoms.

A single covalent bond involves one shared pair of electrons. Some atoms need to share more than one pair: a double bond involves two shared pairs, and a triple bond involves three shared pairs. The number of bonds an atom forms depends on how many more electrons it needs to fill its outer shell.

Key Fact

In covalent bonding, atoms share pairs of electrons. Each atom counts the shared electrons as part of its own outer shell, so both atoms end up with full outer shells. Covalent bonds form between non-metals only.

Hydrogen (H₂): Each hydrogen atom has one electron and needs two for a full first shell. Two hydrogen atoms share one pair of electrons — a single bond.

Water (H₂O): Oxygen has six outer electrons and needs two more. It shares one pair with each of two hydrogen atoms, forming two single bonds. Oxygen also has two lone pairs of electrons that are not shared.

Oxygen (O₂): Each oxygen atom needs two more electrons, so they share two pairs — forming a double bond (O=O).

Methane (CH₄): Carbon has four outer electrons and needs four more. It shares one pair with each of four hydrogen atoms, forming four single bonds.

Nitrogen (N₂): Each nitrogen atom needs three more electrons, so they share three pairs — forming a triple bond. This makes nitrogen gas very stable and unreactive.

Metallic Bonding

metallic bonding is the type of bonding found in metals and alloys. In a metal structure, the atoms are arranged in a regular pattern. The outer shell electrons detach from their atoms and become delocalised electrons — free to move throughout the whole structure. This leaves behind a lattice of positive metal ions surrounded by a “sea” of delocalised electrons.

The strong electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the negative delocalised electrons holds the metal together. This is why metals generally have high melting and boiling points — a lot of energy is needed to overcome these strong forces.

Key Fact

Metallic bonding involves a regular lattice of positive metal ions surrounded by a “sea” of delocalised electrons. The strong electrostatic attraction between the ions and the delocalised electrons explains why metals have high melting points, can conduct electricity, and are malleable.

Comparing the Three Types of Bonding

The type of bonding in a substance depends on the types of atoms involved. Metals bonding with non-metals produce ionic bonds. Non-metals bonding with non-metals produce covalent bonds. Metals bonding with metals produce metallic bonds. Each type involves electrons in a different way, and this directly determines the substance’s properties.

Understanding bonding helps explain physical properties. Ionic compounds have high melting points because of the strong forces between ions in the giant ionic lattice. They conduct electricity when molten or dissolved (because the ions are free to move and carry charge) but not when solid (because the ions are fixed in position). Metals conduct electricity because their delocalised electrons can flow through the structure. Simple covalent molecules generally have low melting points because the forces between molecules are weak, even though the covalent bonds within each molecule are strong.

Use the periodic table: metals are on the left and centre, non-metals are on the right. If the compound contains a metal + non-metal, the bonding is ionic. If it contains non-metals only, the bonding is covalent. If the substance is a pure metal or alloy, the bonding is metallic. For example, NaCl (sodium is a metal, chlorine is a non-metal) = ionic. CO₂ (carbon and oxygen are both non-metals) = covalent. Iron (Fe) = metallic.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When asked to “explain” ionic bonding, always state three things: electrons are transferred (not shared), this forms oppositely charged ions, and there is a strong electrostatic attraction between them. For metallic bonding questions, use the phrase “sea of delocalised electrons” — examiners specifically look for this. If you are asked to draw dot and cross diagrams, only show outer shell electrons, use square brackets around ions, and include the charge.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Ionic bonding — metals transfer electrons to non-metals, forming positive and negative ions held together by strong electrostatic attraction in a giant lattice.
  • Covalent bonding — non-metal atoms share pairs of electrons so both atoms achieve full outer shells. Single, double and triple bonds are all possible.
  • Metallic bonding — positive metal ions are held in a regular lattice by a sea of delocalised electrons, explaining metals’ high melting points and electrical conductivity.

lessons.title: Structure, Properties and Carbon Allotropes
lessons.description: How bonding affects properties, states of matter, and the structures of diamond, graphite and graphene.
lessons.content_html:
States of Matter

All substances exist in one of three states of matter: solid, liquid or gas. The state a substance is in at a given temperature depends on the strength of the forces between its particles. In a solid, particles are held in fixed positions by strong forces and can only vibrate. In a liquid, particles are close together but can move around each other. In a gas, particles are far apart and move quickly in all directions.

Key Fact

You can predict the state of a substance at any temperature using its melting and boiling points. Below its melting point → solid. Between its melting and boiling points → liquid. Above its boiling point → gas.

When a substance changes state, the particles themselves do not change — only the forces between them are overcome. Melting is the change from solid to liquid, boiling (or evaporating) is liquid to gas, freezing is liquid to solid, and condensing is gas to liquid. Sublimation is the direct change from solid to gas without passing through the liquid state.

How Bonding Affects Properties

The properties of a substance depend on its type of bonding and its structure. There are four main types of structure you need to know: giant ionic, simple covalent (small molecules), giant covalent and giant metallic. Each structure gives a substance a distinctive set of physical properties.

Giant ionic lattices (such as sodium chloride) have high melting and boiling points because a large amount of energy is needed to overcome the many strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions. They do not conduct electricity when solid because the ions are held in fixed positions and cannot move. However, they do conduct when molten or dissolved in water because the ions become free to move and carry charge.

Intermolecular forces are the weak forces of attraction between simple covalent molecules. Within each molecule, the covalent bonds are strong, but the forces between molecules are weak. This means simple covalent substances have low melting and boiling points — only a small amount of energy is needed to overcome the intermolecular forces. When a simple covalent substance melts or boils, it is the intermolecular forces that are overcome, not the covalent bonds. Simple covalent substances do not conduct electricity because they have no free electrons or ions to carry charge.

Key Fact

A common exam mistake is saying that covalent bonds break when a simple substance melts or boils. They do not — it is the intermolecular forces between molecules that are overcome, not the strong covalent bonds within the molecules.

Polymers

Polymers are very large molecules made from many small repeating units called monomers joined together in long chains. The intermolecular forces between polymer chains are stronger than those between small molecules because the chains are so long and have many points of contact. This means polymers are generally solid at room temperature. The properties of a polymer depend on the monomers used and the conditions of the reaction.

Giant Covalent Structures

Giant covalent structures contain millions of atoms all bonded to each other by strong covalent bonds in a continuous network. Because of the large number of strong bonds that must be broken, these substances have very high melting and boiling points. They are sometimes called macromolecular structures.

Alloys

Pure metals are relatively soft because the layers of identical atoms can slide over each other easily. An alloy is a mixture of a metal with one or more other elements (usually other metals or carbon). In an alloy, the atoms of different elements are different sizes. This distorts the regular arrangement of metal atoms, preventing the layers from sliding over each other. This is why alloys are harder and stronger than pure metals.

Diamond

Diamond is a form of carbon with a giant covalent structure. Each carbon atom forms four strong covalent bonds with other carbon atoms in a rigid tetrahedral arrangement. This makes diamond extremely hard — in fact, it is the hardest known natural substance. Diamond has a very high melting point because many strong covalent bonds must be broken. It does not conduct electricity because all four outer electrons on each carbon atom are used in bonding — there are no free electrons or delocalised electrons to carry charge.

Graphite

Graphite is another form of carbon with a giant covalent structure, but its structure is very different from diamond. In graphite, each carbon atom bonds to only three other carbon atoms, forming flat hexagonal layers. This leaves one electron on each carbon atom free to become delocalised between the layers.

Key Fact

Graphite is unusual for a non-metal because it conducts electricity. Each carbon atom has one delocalised electron that is free to move along the layers and carry charge. The layers are held together by weak intermolecular forces, so they can slide over each other easily — this is why graphite is soft and slippery, and is used in pencils and as a lubricant.

Graphene and Fullerenes

Graphene is a single layer of graphite — a sheet of carbon atoms arranged in hexagons, just one atom thick. Despite being so thin, graphene is incredibly strong and is an excellent conductor of electricity and heat. It has potential applications in electronics, composite materials and energy storage.

Fullerenes are molecules of carbon atoms arranged in hollow shapes. The most well-known fullerene is buckminsterfullerene (C₆₀), which has 60 carbon atoms arranged in a sphere made of hexagons and pentagons — like a football. Carbon nanotubes are cylindrical fullerenes with very high length-to-diameter ratios. They have remarkable properties: they are very strong, are excellent conductors of electricity and heat, and can be used to strengthen composite materials, in electronics and in drug delivery systems.

Allotropes are different structural forms of the same element. Diamond, graphite, graphene and fullerenes are all allotropes of carbon — they are all made entirely of carbon atoms, but arranged in different ways. This is why they have such different properties:

  • Diamond: each carbon bonded to 4 others → very hard, does not conduct electricity.
  • Graphite: each carbon bonded to 3 others in layers → soft, slippery, conducts electricity.
  • Graphene: single layer of graphite → strong, flexible, conducts electricity and heat.
  • Fullerenes: hollow spheres or tubes → can trap molecules inside, used in drug delivery and composites.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When explaining properties of giant covalent substances, always state that there are many strong covalent bonds that require a large amount of energy to break. For graphite, you must explain that it conducts electricity because of delocalised electrons between the layers — not because it contains “free ions.” In compare questions about diamond and graphite, structure your answer around the number of bonds per carbon atom (4 vs 3) and whether delocalised electrons are present.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The properties of a substance depend on its type of bonding and structure. Simple covalent substances have low melting points (weak intermolecular forces), while giant covalent and ionic structures have very high melting points (many strong bonds or forces to overcome).
  • Diamond has four covalent bonds per carbon atom making it very hard and non-conducting, while graphite has three bonds per carbon with one delocalised electron per atom, making it soft, slippery and electrically conductive.
  • Graphene is a single layer of graphite with exceptional strength and conductivity. Fullerenes are hollow carbon molecules with applications in drug delivery, electronics and composite materials.

• This prevents layers from sliding, making the alloy harder and stronger than the pure metal.

lessons.title: Quantitative Chemistry: Mass, Moles and Concentrations
lessons.description: Conservation of mass, relative formula mass, moles and concentration calculations.
lessons.content_html:
Conservation of Mass

In every chemical reaction, the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products. This is the law of conservation of mass. It holds because no atoms are created or destroyed during a chemical reaction — they are simply rearranged into new substances.

A balanced symbol equation proves this: the number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides. For example, in 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O there are four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms on each side. If the total relative atomic mass of the reactant atoms is calculated, it will match the total for the product atoms exactly.

Key Fact

No atoms are created or destroyed in a chemical reaction. The total mass of reactants always equals the total mass of products. Any apparent change in mass on a balance is caused by a gas entering or leaving the system.

If a reaction takes place in an open container, the mass reading on a balance may appear to change. When a gas is produced — for example, carbon dioxide from calcium carbonate reacting with hydrochloric acid — the gas escapes and the balance reading decreases. When a metal burns in air — for example, magnesium combining with oxygen — the product (magnesium oxide) is heavier than the original metal because oxygen atoms from the air have been added, so the balance reading increases. In both cases mass is still conserved when the entire system (including any gas that escaped or entered) is considered.

A balanced equation shows the conservation of mass in symbol form. If the equation is not balanced, it implies atoms have appeared from nowhere or vanished — which cannot happen. When balancing, you adjust the large numbers (coefficients) in front of formulae, never the small subscript numbers inside a formula. Changing a subscript would change the substance itself.

Relative Formula Mass (Mr)

The relative formula mass (Mr) of a compound is calculated by adding up the relative atomic masses (Ar) of every atom in its formula. Ar values are found on the periodic table. Mr has no units because it is a ratio compared to one-twelfth the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

Worked example — sodium hydroxide (NaOH): Ar values: Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1. Mr = 23 + 16 + 1 = 40.

Worked example — calcium carbonate (CaCO3): Ar values: Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16. Mr = 40 + 12 + (3 × 16) = 100.

When a formula contains brackets, the subscript outside the bracket multiplies every atom inside. In Mg(OH)2: there is 1 Mg, 2 O and 2 H. Ar values: Mg = 24, O = 16, H = 1. Mr = 24 + 2 × (16 + 1) = 24 + 34 = 58. Another example: Ca(NO3)2 has 1 Ca, 2 N and 6 O. Mr = 40 + (2 × 14) + (6 × 16) = 40 + 28 + 96 = 164.

The Mole and Avogadro’s Constant

The mole (mol) is the unit chemists use to count particles. One mole of any substance contains exactly 6.02 × 1023 particles — this number is called Avogadro’s constant. Whether counting atoms, molecules or ions, the number is always the same.

The mass of one mole of a substance (in grams) equals its Mr. For instance, Mr of water (H2O) is 18, so one mole of water has a mass of 18 g. The key equation linking mass and moles is:

Key Fact

\(moles = mass (g) \div M_{r}\). Rearranged: mass = moles × Mr, or Mr = mass ÷ moles. This equation is on the AQA equation sheet — practise rearranging it.

Example 1: How many moles in 11 g of CO2? Mr of CO2 = 12 + (2 × 16) = 44. Moles = 11 ÷ 44 = 0.25 mol.

Example 2: What is the mass of 3 mol of NaOH (Mr = 40)? Mass = 3 × 40 = 120 g.

Example 3: How many moles in 5.6 g of nitrogen gas (N2, Mr = 28)? Moles = 5.6 ÷ 28 = 0.2 mol. Always use Mr of the molecule, not Ar of a single atom.

Reacting Masses from Balanced Equations

A balanced equation tells you the mole ratio of reactants and products. This ratio lets you calculate the mass of any substance in the reaction if you know the mass of another. Follow these four steps:

Step 1: Write the balanced equation. Step 2: Calculate moles of the substance you know (moles = mass ÷ Mr). Step 3: Use the mole ratio from the equation to find moles of the substance you want. Step 4: Convert moles back to mass (mass = moles × Mr).

Question: What mass of iron is produced when 480 g of iron oxide (Fe2O3) reacts with carbon? The equation is: 2Fe2O3 + 3C → 4Fe + 3CO2.

Step 1: Equation already balanced. Step 2: Mr of Fe2O3 = (2 × 56) + (3 × 16) = 160. Moles of Fe2O3 = 480 ÷ 160 = 3 mol. Step 3: Ratio is 2 mol Fe2O3 : 4 mol Fe. So 3 mol Fe2O3 produces 6 mol Fe. Step 4: Mass of Fe = 6 × 56 = 336 g.

Limiting Reactants and Excess

In most practical reactions, one reactant is used up before the other. The limiting reactant is the one completely used up first — it determines how much product can be formed. The other reactant is in excess because some of it is left unreacted.

To identify the limiting reactant: calculate the moles of each reactant, then compare these to the mole ratio in the balanced equation. The reactant that provides fewer moles relative to its required ratio is the limiting reactant. Adding more of the limiting reactant increases the amount of product; adding more of the excess reactant makes no difference.

Key Fact

The limiting reactant controls how much product is made. Once it is used up, the reaction stops — even if there is plenty of the other reactant remaining. To make more product, add more of the limiting reactant.

Concentration of Solutions

A solution forms when a solute dissolves in a solvent. The concentration tells you how much solute is dissolved per unit volume of solution.

At GCSE you need to calculate concentration in grams per decimetre cubed: \(concentration (g/dm^{3})\,=\,\text{mass of solute} (g)\, \div \,\text{volume of solution} (dm^{3})\). Remember that 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³. Always convert cm³ to dm³ by dividing by 1000 before substituting into the equation.

Example 1: 10 g of sodium chloride is dissolved in 250 cm³ of water. What is the concentration? Volume = 250 ÷ 1000 = 0.25 dm³. Concentration = 10 ÷ 0.25 = 40 g/dm³.

Example 2: A solution has a concentration of 80 g/dm³ and a volume of 500 cm³. What mass of solute does it contain? Volume = 0.5 dm³. Mass = concentration × volume = 80 × 0.5 = 40 g.

Increasing the mass of solute in the same volume makes the solution more concentrated. Adding more solvent without adding more solute makes it more dilute. Concentration links directly to rates of reaction: a higher concentration means more solute particles per unit volume, leading to more frequent collisions between reactant particles and therefore a faster reaction rate.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Calculation questions on quantitative chemistry are worth 2–3 marks each. Always show your working — even if your final answer is wrong, you can earn method marks. Write the equation you are using, substitute values with units, then state your answer with correct units. For Mr questions, write out each Ar value and show the multiplication. For reacting mass problems, follow the four-step method: balanced equation → moles of known → mole ratio → mass of unknown. For concentration, check whether the volume is in cm³ or dm³ before you begin.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Conservation of mass means no atoms are created or destroyed in a reaction — any apparent mass change on a balance is caused by a gas entering or leaving the open system.
  • Mr is the sum of all Ar values in a formula. Moles = mass (g) ÷ Mr. Use mole ratios from balanced equations to calculate reacting masses using the four-step method.
  • The limiting reactant is used up first and controls how much product forms. Concentration (g/dm³) = mass of solute ÷ volume of solution.

lessons.title: Reactivity of Metals and Metal Extraction
lessons.description: The reactivity series, displacement reactions, and how metals are extracted from their ores.
lessons.content_html:
Metal Oxides

Metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides. For example, magnesium burns brightly in air to form magnesium oxide:

\(2Mg + O₂ \rightarrow 2MgO\)

Most metal oxides are bases. This means they react with acids to form a salt and water. Some metal oxides dissolve in water to form alkaline solutions — for example, sodium oxide dissolves in water to produce sodium hydroxide. However, not all metal oxides are basic: aluminium oxide and zinc oxide are amphoteric — they can react with both acids and alkalis.

Key Fact

Most metal oxides are bases. Some, like sodium oxide and potassium oxide, dissolve in water to form alkaline solutions. Aluminium oxide and zinc oxide are amphoteric — they react with both acids and bases.

The Reactivity Series

The reactivity series ranks metals from most reactive to least reactive. The more reactive a metal is, the more easily it loses electrons to form positive ions.

From most reactive to least reactive, the series runs: potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, carbon, zinc, iron, tin, lead, hydrogen, copper, silver, gold, platinum. Carbon and hydrogen are included as reference points even though they are not metals.

The reactivity series is established by observing how metals react with water and dilute acids. Metals like potassium and sodium react violently with cold water. Magnesium reacts slowly with cold water but vigorously with steam. Metals like iron and zinc only react with steam. Copper, silver and gold do not react with water or dilute acids at all — they are the least reactive.

Displacement Reactions

A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from its compound. For example, if iron is added to copper sulfate solution, the iron displaces the copper:

\(Fe + CuSO₄ \rightarrow FeSO₄ + Cu\)

You would observe the blue copper sulfate solution turning pale green (iron sulfate) and an orange-brown coating of copper appearing on the iron. This confirms that iron is more reactive than copper.

Key Fact

A more reactive metal will displace a less reactive metal from a solution of its salt. This is the basis of displacement reactions, and it is how the reactivity series is confirmed experimentally.

The thermite reaction is a dramatic displacement reaction. Aluminium powder reacts with iron(III) oxide to produce molten iron and aluminium oxide: \(2Al + Fe₂O₃ \rightarrow Al₂O₃ + 2Fe\). This works because aluminium is more reactive than iron. The reaction is so exothermic that the iron produced is molten. It is used to weld railway tracks together.

Extraction of Metals

Metals are found in the Earth’s crust, mostly as ores — rocks that contain enough metal compound to make extraction worthwhile. The method used to extract a metal depends on its position in the reactivity series.

Unreactive metals like gold and platinum exist naturally as pure elements because they do not easily react with other substances. Most other metals must be chemically separated from their ores.

Metals below carbon in the reactivity series (zinc, iron, tin, lead, copper) can be extracted by reduction with carbon. Carbon is more reactive than these metals, so it displaces them from their oxides. Metals above carbon in the reactivity series (potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium) are too reactive to be extracted by carbon — they must be extracted using electrolysis, which is more expensive because it uses large amounts of electricity.

Reduction with Carbon

Iron is extracted from its ore, iron oxide (Fe₂O₃), in a blast furnace. Coke (a form of carbon) is burned with hot air to produce carbon monoxide, which then reduces the iron oxide:

\(Fe₂O₃ + 3CO \rightarrow 2Fe + 3CO₂\)

The iron oxide has been reduced because it has lost oxygen. The carbon monoxide has been oxidised because it has gained oxygen. This is a redox reaction — reduction and oxidation happen simultaneously.

Key Fact

Metals less reactive than carbon are extracted by reduction with carbon. Metals more reactive than carbon must be extracted by electrolysis. The position of carbon in the reactivity series is the dividing line.

Oxidation and Reduction in Terms of Electrons (Higher Tier)

Oxidation is the loss of electrons. Reduction is the gain of electrons. The memory aid OIL RIG helps: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).

In the reaction between iron and copper sulfate:

\(Fe \rightarrow Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻\) (iron is oxidised — it loses electrons)

\(Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ \rightarrow Cu\) (copper is reduced — it gains electrons)

More reactive metals have a stronger tendency to lose their outer electrons and form positive ions. This is because their outer electrons are further from the nucleus and are more easily removed. Potassium, for example, loses its single outer electron very easily, which is why it reacts so vigorously. Gold holds onto its electrons tightly, which is why it barely reacts at all — and why it is valued for jewellery and electronics.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When explaining why a displacement reaction occurs, always refer to the reactivity series: state which metal is more reactive and explain that it displaces the less reactive metal. For higher tier, use the terms oxidation and reduction in terms of electron transfer — remember OIL RIG. In extended response questions on metal extraction, link the extraction method (carbon reduction or electrolysis) to the metal’s position in the reactivity series relative to carbon.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The reactivity series ranks metals by how readily they react — more reactive metals lose electrons more easily and can displace less reactive metals from their compounds.
  • Metals below carbon in the reactivity series are extracted by reduction with carbon (e.g. iron in the blast furnace). Metals above carbon require electrolysis.
  • Oxidation is the loss of electrons (OIL); reduction is the gain of electrons (RIG). A reaction where both occur is called a redox reaction.

lessons.title: Reactions of Acids, pH and Neutralisation
lessons.description: How acids react with metals, bases and carbonates, plus the pH scale and strong vs weak acids.
lessons.content_html:
Reactions of Acids with Metals

When an acid reacts with a metal, the products are a salt and hydrogen gas. The general word equation is:

Key Fact

acid + metal → salt + hydrogen

For example, magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid to produce magnesium chloride and hydrogen: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. The hydrogen gas can be tested with a burning splint — it burns with a squeaky pop.

Not all metals react with acids. Only metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series will displace hydrogen from an acid. Unreactive metals such as copper and gold do not react with dilute acids.

Neutralisation Reactions

Neutralisation occurs when an acid reacts with a base. The general equation is:

Key Fact

acid + base → salt + water

A base is any substance that reacts with an acid to form a salt and water. If a base dissolves in water, it is called an alkali. The ionic equation for all neutralisation reactions is: H+(aq) + OH−(aq) → H₂O(l).

When acids react with metal carbonates, three products form: a salt, water and carbon dioxide gas. The general equation is: acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide. For instance, calcium carbonate reacts with hydrochloric acid: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂.

The name of the salt produced depends on the acid used and the metal or base involved. Hydrochloric acid always produces chloride salts (e.g. sodium chloride). Sulfuric acid always produces sulfate salts (e.g. copper sulfate). Nitric acid always produces nitrate salts (e.g. potassium nitrate).

The first part of the salt’s name comes from the metal or the metal in the base. For example, sodium hydroxide + hydrochloric acid → sodium chloride + water.

Making Soluble Salts

In the required practical, you make a pure, dry sample of a soluble salt by reacting an insoluble base or carbonate with an acid. The steps are:

1. Warm the acid gently in a beaker. 2. Add the insoluble base (e.g. copper oxide) in small amounts, stirring after each addition, until it is in excess — you know it is in excess when unreacted solid remains at the bottom. 3. Filter the mixture to remove the excess solid. 4. Pour the filtrate into an evaporating basin and heat gently until crystals begin to form at the edges. 5. Leave the solution to cool and allow crystals to form by slow evaporation. 6. Pat the crystals dry with filter paper.

Adding an excess of the insoluble reactant ensures all the acid has reacted. This is important because any remaining acid would contaminate the salt crystals. The excess solid is simply removed by filtration, leaving a pure salt solution behind.

The pH Scale and Indicators

The pH scale runs from 0 to 14. A pH below 7 is acidic, pH 7 is neutral, and a pH above 7 is alkaline. The lower the pH, the more acidic the solution; the higher the pH, the more alkaline.

An indicator is used to measure pH. Litmus paper gives a simple acid/alkali test (red = acidic, blue = alkaline). Universal indicator gives a colour for every pH value, providing more detail. A pH meter gives the most precise reading.

Key Fact

During neutralisation, hydrogen ions (H+) from the acid react with hydroxide ions (OH−) from the alkali to produce water. As the acid is neutralised, the pH rises towards 7.

Strong and Weak Acids (Higher Tier)

A strong acid is one that completely ionises in water — every molecule splits into ions. Examples include hydrochloric acid (HCl), sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄) and nitric acid (HNO₃).

A weak acid only partially ionises in water. The ionisation is reversible and an equilibrium is established, meaning only a small fraction of the acid molecules release hydrogen ions at any given time. Examples include ethanoic acid (vinegar) and citric acid (in citrus fruits).

Students often confuse concentration and strength. Concentration is the amount of acid dissolved in a given volume of water (measured in mol/dm³). Strength is about how much the acid ionises. A weak acid can be concentrated (lots of it dissolved) but still weak (only partially ionised). A strong acid can be dilute (small amount dissolved) but still strong (fully ionised).

As a strong acid is diluted, its pH increases towards 7 but it remains a strong acid. The pH of a strong acid is always lower than a weak acid of the same concentration, because the strong acid releases more H+ ions.

A titration is used to find the exact volume of acid needed to neutralise a measured volume of alkali (or vice versa). The alkali is placed in a conical flask with a few drops of indicator. Acid is added from a burette, one drop at a time near the end point, until the indicator changes colour. The experiment is repeated until concordant results (within 0.10 cm³) are obtained. The mean titre is then calculated, discarding any anomalous results.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions about acid reactions, always name the salt produced — examiners award marks for correctly identifying it from the acid and metal/base used. For higher tier, make sure you can clearly explain the difference between strong and weak acids using the terms ‘fully ionised’ and ‘partially ionised’, and never confuse strength with concentration.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Acids react with metals to produce a salt and hydrogen, with bases to produce a salt and water, and with carbonates to produce a salt, water and carbon dioxide.
  • The pH scale runs from 0 (strongly acidic) to 14 (strongly alkaline), with 7 being neutral. Neutralisation increases the pH of an acid towards 7.
  • Strong acids fully ionise in water; weak acids only partially ionise. Strength and concentration are different concepts.

lessons.title: Electrolysis
lessons.description: How electrolysis breaks down ionic compounds, extracts metals, and produces useful products.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Electrolysis?

electrolysis is the process of using an electric current to decompose an ionic compound into its elements. It only works when the compound is either molten (melted) or dissolved in water, because the ions must be free to move and carry the current. In a solid ionic compound the ions are locked in a fixed lattice and cannot move, so no current flows.

The substance being broken down is called the electrolyte. During electrolysis, the electrolyte is connected to a direct current (d.c.) power supply via two electrodes — usually made of inert materials such as graphite or platinum so they do not react with the products.

Key Fact

Electrolysis requires a d.c. supply. The positive electrode is called the anode and the negative electrode is called the cathode. Positive ions (cations) migrate to the cathode; negative ions (anions) migrate to the anode.

What Happens at the Electrodes?

During electrolysis, positive ions are attracted to the negative electrode (cathode) and negative ions are attracted to the positive electrode (anode). When the ions reach the electrodes, they gain or lose electrons and are discharged as atoms or molecules.

At the cathode, positive ions gain electrons — this is reduction. At the anode, negative ions lose electrons — this is oxidation. A useful mnemonic is OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).

Molten lead bromide (PbBr₂) contains Pb²⁺ and Br⁻ ions that are free to move. When a current passes through:

At the cathode (negative electrode): Pb²⁺ ions gain two electrons and are reduced to form lead metal. Half equation (HT): Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb

At the anode (positive electrode): Br⁻ ions lose electrons and are oxidised to form bromine gas. Half equation (HT): 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻

Electrolysis of Molten Ionic Compounds

When an ionic compound is melted, only two types of ion are present — the metal ion and the non-metal ion. This makes predicting products straightforward: the metal always forms at the cathode and the non-metal always forms at the anode.

For example, molten sodium chloride (NaCl) contains Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. Sodium metal forms at the cathode (Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na) and chlorine gas forms at the anode (2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻). Molten aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃) produces aluminium at the cathode and oxygen at the anode.

Extracting Aluminium by Electrolysis

Aluminium is too reactive to be extracted from its ore by carbon reduction, so electrolysis is used instead. The ore is bauxite, which is purified to give aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃). Pure aluminium oxide has a very high melting point (over 2000 °C), which would be extremely expensive to maintain.

To solve this, aluminium oxide is dissolved in molten cryolite (Na₃AlF₆), which lowers the melting point to about 950 °C and reduces energy costs significantly.

Key Fact

In aluminium extraction: at the cathode, Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al (reduction). At the anode, 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻ (oxidation). The graphite anodes gradually burn away because they react with the oxygen produced (C + O₂ → CO₂), so they must be replaced regularly.

Aluminium extraction is expensive because it requires a continuous supply of electricity to keep the mixture molten and to drive the electrolysis. This is why aluminium recycling is so important — recycling uses only about 5% of the energy needed to extract aluminium from bauxite.

Electrolysis of Aqueous Solutions

When an ionic compound is dissolved in water, the situation is more complicated. Water itself breaks down into H⁺ and OH⁻ ions, so the solution contains four types of ion: the metal ion and the non-metal ion from the compound, plus H⁺ and OH⁻ from water. This means there is a competition at each electrode to decide which ion is discharged.

At the cathode (negative electrode): If the metal is less reactive than hydrogen (e.g. copper, silver, gold, platinum), the metal is deposited. If the metal is more reactive than hydrogen (e.g. sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc), hydrogen gas is produced instead.

At the anode (positive electrode): If the solution contains halide ions (Cl⁻, Br⁻, or I⁻), the halogen is produced. If no halide ions are present, oxygen gas is produced (from the discharge of OH⁻ ions).

For example, electrolysis of copper sulfate solution (CuSO₄(aq)) produces copper at the cathode (because copper is less reactive than hydrogen) and oxygen at the anode (because sulfate ions are not halide ions, so OH⁻ ions are discharged instead).

Electrolysis of Brine (Sodium Chloride Solution)

The electrolysis of brine is one of the most important industrial applications of electrolysis. Brine contains Na⁺, H⁺, Cl⁻, and OH⁻ ions. Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen gas is produced at the cathode. Chloride is a halide ion, so chlorine gas is produced at the anode. The ions left in solution — Na⁺ and OH⁻ — form sodium hydroxide solution.

Key Fact

The three products of brine electrolysis all have important industrial uses. Chlorine: making PVC, bleach, and disinfecting water. Hydrogen: making margarine and as a fuel. Sodium hydroxide: making soap, paper, and bleach.

Half Equations (Higher Tier)

half equations show the reaction at each individual electrode. At the cathode, ions gain electrons (reduction); at the anode, ions lose electrons (oxidation). The number of electrons must balance the charge on the ion.

Cathode (reduction — gain of electrons):

Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na • Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu • Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al • 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂

Anode (oxidation — loss of electrons):

2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ • 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻ • 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻ • 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻

In Required Practical 3, you investigate what happens when different aqueous solutions are electrolysed using inert (carbon) electrodes. You observe and test the products at each electrode. For example, bubbles at the cathode can be tested with a burning splint (a squeaky pop confirms hydrogen). A damp litmus paper held near the anode turns white if chlorine is produced, or the gas relights a glowing splint if it is oxygen.

You should be able to explain your results using the rules for predicting products: metal reactivity compared to hydrogen at the cathode, and the presence or absence of halide ions at the anode.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions on electrolysis, always state which ion goes to which electrode and why (opposite charges attract). If asked to write half equations, check the total charge balances on both sides. Remember that “explain” questions need a reason, not just a fact — for example, “hydrogen is produced at the cathode because sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so H⁺ ions are discharged instead.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Electrolysis decomposes ionic compounds using electricity — the electrolyte must be molten or dissolved so ions can move. Reduction (gain of electrons) occurs at the cathode; oxidation (loss of electrons) occurs at the anode.
  • For molten compounds, the metal forms at the cathode and the non-metal at the anode. For aqueous solutions, reactivity determines whether the metal or hydrogen is produced at the cathode, and halide ions determine whether a halogen or oxygen forms at the anode.
  • Brine electrolysis produces three useful products: chlorine (anode), hydrogen (cathode), and sodium hydroxide (left in solution). Aluminium is extracted from bauxite dissolved in cryolite to lower the melting point.

lessons.title: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions
lessons.description: Exothermic and endothermic reactions, reaction profiles, and bond energy calculations.
lessons.content_html:
Energy Changes in Reactions

Every chemical reaction involves a transfer of energy between the reacting substances and their surroundings. Some reactions release energy — making the surroundings hotter — while others absorb energy, making the surroundings cooler. Understanding these energy changes is essential for explaining everyday processes, from hand warmers to cold packs, and for predicting whether a reaction will happen on its own.

Exothermic Reactions

An exothermic reaction is one that transfers energy to the surroundings. The surroundings get hotter, so a thermometer placed in the reaction mixture would show a temperature rise. The energy is usually transferred as heat, but sometimes as light, sound or electrical energy.

Common examples of exothermic reactions include:

  • Combustion — burning fuels like methane or wood releases heat and light energy.
  • Neutralisation — when an acid reacts with an alkali, the solution warms up.
  • Oxidation reactions — such as respiration in cells or the rusting of iron.
  • Hand warmers — disposable hand warmers use an exothermic reaction (often iron oxidation) to release heat slowly.
Key Fact

In an exothermic reaction, the products have less energy than the reactants. The “missing” energy has been transferred to the surroundings, which is why the temperature rises.

Endothermic Reactions

An endothermic reaction is the opposite — it takes in energy from the surroundings. The surroundings get cooler, so a thermometer would show a temperature drop.

Common examples of endothermic reactions include:

  • Thermal decomposition — calcium carbonate must be heated continuously to break down into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide.
  • Citric acid and sodium hydrogen carbonate — dissolving these together in water causes the temperature to fall.
  • Sports cold packs — instant cold packs contain ammonium nitrate and water, separated by a barrier. When the barrier is broken, the endothermic dissolving process absorbs heat from the injured area.
  • Photosynthesis — plants absorb light energy from the sun to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose.
Key Fact

In an endothermic reaction, the products have more energy than the reactants. Energy has been taken in from the surroundings, which is why the temperature falls.

In this required practical, you investigate the temperature change when different combinations of chemicals are mixed. A polystyrene cup is used as a simple calorimeter because it is a good insulator — it minimises heat loss to the surroundings.

Method: measure a known volume of acid into the cup, record the starting temperature, add a measured amount of alkali or metal powder, stir gently, and record the highest (exothermic) or lowest (endothermic) temperature reached. The temperature change (ΔT) tells you the energy transferred.

Key variables: the independent variable is the type of chemical added, the dependent variable is the temperature change, and control variables include the volume and concentration of acid, starting temperature, and the insulation used.

Reaction Profiles

A reaction profile is a diagram that shows how the energy of the reactants and products compares, and the energy route the reaction takes. The y-axis shows energy and the x-axis shows the progress of the reaction.

Exothermic Reaction Profile

On an exothermic reaction profile, the reactants start at a higher energy level than the products. The difference between the two levels is the overall energy change — this energy is released to the surroundings. There is always a “hill” that the reaction must climb first. The height of this hill above the reactants is the activation energy (Ea) — the minimum energy particles need to collide successfully and start the reaction.

Endothermic Reaction Profile

On an endothermic reaction profile, the products are at a higher energy level than the reactants. The overall energy change is taken in from the surroundings. The activation energy hill is still present — endothermic reactions still need an initial energy input to get started, and the overall energy absorbed is shown by the gap between the product and reactant levels.

Key Fact

A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy. On a reaction profile, a catalyst is shown as a second, lower curve — the reactant and product energy levels stay the same, but the hill is shorter.

When reading a reaction profile in the exam, you should be able to identify: (1) whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic by comparing the energy levels of reactants and products, (2) the activation energy as the height from the reactants to the top of the curve, and (3) the overall energy change as the difference between reactant and product energy levels.

When drawing a reaction profile, always label both axes (energy on the y-axis, progress of reaction on the x-axis), mark the reactants and products at the correct levels, draw a smooth curve over the top (not a pointed peak), and label the activation energy and overall energy change with arrows.

Bond Energy Calculations (Higher Tier)

During a chemical reaction, bonds in the reactants must be broken and new bonds in the products must be made. Breaking bonds requires energy (it is endothermic), and making bonds releases energy (it is exothermic). The overall energy change of a reaction depends on the balance between these two processes.

The bond energy is the amount of energy needed to break one mole of a particular type of bond (measured in kJ/mol). The same amount of energy is released when that bond forms. Bond energies are given in data tables in the exam — you do not need to memorise them.

Key Fact

Overall energy change = \(\text{energy to break bonds} (\text{in reactants}) - \text{energy released making bonds} (\text{in products})\). If the answer is positive, the reaction is endothermic. If the answer is negative, the reaction is exothermic.

Calculate the overall energy change for the reaction: H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl

Step 1 — identify bonds broken: One H–H bond (436 kJ/mol) and one Cl–Cl bond (242 kJ/mol). Total energy to break bonds = 436 + 242 = 678 kJ/mol.

Step 2 — identify bonds made: Two H–Cl bonds (431 kJ/mol each). Total energy released making bonds = 2 × 431 = 862 kJ/mol.

Step 3 — calculate overall energy change: 678 − 862 = \(- 184 kJ/mol\). The negative sign means the reaction is exothermic — more energy is released making bonds than is needed to break them.

Students often lose marks by: (1) forgetting to count all the bonds — for example, CH4 has four C–H bonds, not one; (2) subtracting the wrong way round — it is always bonds broken minus bonds made; (3) confusing the sign — a negative answer means exothermic, positive means endothermic; (4) not using the displayed formula to count bonds accurately.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When asked to explain whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic, always link the direction of energy transfer to the temperature change in the surroundings — saying “energy is released” is not enough on its own. For bond energy calculations, show every step: list bonds broken, list bonds made, then subtract. The examiner awards method marks, so even if your final answer is wrong, you can still pick up marks for a clear working method.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Exothermic reactions transfer energy to the surroundings (temperature rises); endothermic reactions take in energy from the surroundings (temperature falls).
  • Reaction profiles show the relative energy of reactants and products, and the activation energy needed to start the reaction.
  • Overall energy change = energy to break bonds − energy released making bonds. A negative value is exothermic; a positive value is endothermic.

lessons.title: Transition Metals and Nanoparticles
lessons.description: Properties of transition metals vs Group 1, and how nanoparticles differ from bulk materials.
lessons.content_html:
Transition Metals in the Periodic Table

The transition metals sit in the central block of the periodic table, between Group 2 and Group 3. Common examples include iron (Fe), copper (Cu), nickel (Ni), chromium (Cr), cobalt (Co), platinum (Pt), and gold (Au). Unlike the metals in Group 1, transition metals are much harder, stronger, denser, and have much higher melting points — making them far more useful as structural and engineering materials.

Transition metals are good conductors of heat and electricity, which is why copper is used for electrical wiring and iron is the main component in steel for buildings and bridges. They are also much less reactive than Group 1 metals, so they do not react vigorously with water or oxygen at room temperature.

Key Fact

Transition metals have higher melting points, higher densities, and are harder and stronger than Group 1 metals. They are also much less reactive — they do not react vigorously with water or oxygen.

Comparing Transition Metals with Group 1

The specification requires you to compare transition metals directly with Group 1 metals (the alkali metals: lithium, sodium, potassium). The differences arise because transition metals have more electrons available for bonding and their metallic bonds are stronger.

Hardness: Transition metals are hard and tough (iron is used in construction). Group 1 metals are so soft they can be cut with a knife.

Density: Transition metals are dense (iron = 7.9 g/cm³). Group 1 metals have low densities — lithium, sodium, and potassium all float on water.

Melting point: Transition metals have high melting points (iron melts at 1538 °C, copper at 1085 °C). Group 1 metals melt at much lower temperatures (sodium melts at just 98 °C).

Reactivity: Transition metals react slowly or not at all with water and oxygen. Group 1 metals react vigorously — potassium bursts into lilac flames when placed on water.

Special Properties of Transition Metals

Two properties of transition metals are frequently tested in the exam: their ability to act as catalysts and their tendency to form coloured compounds.

Catalysts: Many transition metals and their compounds are used as catalysts in industrial reactions. Iron is the catalyst in the Haber process (making ammonia), nickel is used in the hydrogenation of vegetable oils to make margarine, and platinum is used in catalytic converters in car exhausts to reduce harmful emissions. Catalysts speed up reactions without being used up themselves, lowering the activation energy needed for the reaction to occur.

Coloured compounds: Unlike Group 1 metals, which form white or colourless compounds, transition metals form compounds with distinctive colours. Copper sulfate is blue, iron(II) compounds are green, iron(III) compounds are orange-brown, and potassium dichromate is orange. These colours are useful in identifying unknown substances during chemical analysis.

Key Fact

Transition metals can form ions with different charges (e.g. Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺), which is why iron forms both green iron(II) compounds and orange-brown iron(III) compounds. Group 1 metals only form ions with a +1 charge.

What Are Nanoparticles?

Nanoparticles are extremely small structures with dimensions between 1 and 100 nanometres (nm). A single nanometre is one billionth of a metre (1 nm = 1 × 10⁻9 m). To put this in perspective, a human hair is around 80,000 nm wide, so nanoparticles are roughly a thousand times smaller. They typically contain a few hundred to a few thousand atoms.

Nanoparticles are much smaller than fine particles (1 µm – 2.5 µm) and coarse particles (larger than 2.5 µm, often called dust). The spec expects you to understand the size scale: coarse > fine > nanoparticles.

Surface Area to Volume Ratio

The key reason nanoparticles behave differently from the same material in bulk is their very high surface area to volume ratio. As a particle gets smaller, its surface area increases relative to its volume. This means a much greater proportion of the atoms are on the surface, where they can interact with other substances.

You can demonstrate this with a simple cube calculation. A cube with sides of 1 cm has a surface area of 6 cm² and a volume of 1 cm³, giving a ratio of 6:1. If you cut that same cube into smaller cubes with sides of 0.1 cm, the total surface area increases to 60 cm² while the total volume stays at 1 cm³ — a ratio of 60:1. At the nanoscale, this ratio becomes enormous.

Key Fact

As particle size decreases, the surface area to volume ratio increases. This is why nanoparticles have different properties from the same material in bulk — more atoms are exposed on the surface, making them more reactive and more effective as catalysts, coatings, and drug delivery agents.

A cube has sides of 2 cm. Calculate its surface area to volume ratio.

Surface area = 6 × (2 × 2) = 24 cm². Volume = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 cm³. Ratio = 24 ÷ 8 = 3:1.

Now a cube with sides of 0.5 cm. Surface area = 6 × (0.5 × 0.5) = 1.5 cm². Volume = 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.125 cm³. Ratio = 1.5 ÷ 0.125 = 12:1.

The smaller cube has a surface area to volume ratio four times greater than the larger one. At the nanoscale, this ratio is thousands of times larger still.

Uses of Nanoparticles

Because of their high surface area to volume ratio, nanoparticles have properties that make them useful in a range of applications. The spec highlights several key uses.

Sunscreens: Titanium dioxide and zinc oxide nanoparticles are used in sunscreens. In bulk form these chemicals are white and leave a visible white layer on the skin. As nanoparticles they are transparent — they still absorb and reflect harmful UV radiation but cannot be seen, making the product more cosmetically appealing.

Catalysts: Nanoparticles of metals such as gold and platinum can act as highly efficient catalysts because their enormous surface area provides many more active sites for reactions to take place. Less material is needed compared to using the bulk metal, reducing costs.

Medicine: Nanoparticles can be used for targeted drug delivery — carrying medication directly to diseased cells (such as cancer cells) while minimising side effects to healthy tissue. Silver nanoparticles have antibacterial properties and are used in wound dressings and medical equipment coatings.

Electronics and coatings: Nanoparticles are used in electronics to build smaller, more powerful components. They are also used in self-cleaning glass coatings and antibacterial surfaces.

Nanoparticles are so small that they may be able to enter cells and pass through membranes that larger particles cannot cross, including the blood–brain barrier. There are concerns that inhaling nanoparticles could damage the lungs in a similar way to asbestos fibres. Because nanoparticles are a relatively new technology, their long-term effects on human health and the environment are not yet fully understood. Scientists continue to research whether nanoparticles in sunscreens, food packaging, and other consumer products pose any risk when absorbed through the skin or ingested.

The exam may ask you to evaluate the use of nanoparticles — meaning you need to weigh up the benefits (better sunscreens, targeted medicine, efficient catalysts) against the potential risks (unknown long-term health effects, environmental concerns).
lessons.exam_tip_html: When comparing transition metals with Group 1 metals, always state the specific property and give an example for each side — for instance, “iron has a melting point of 1538 °C compared with sodium at 98 °C.” For nanoparticle questions, the key phrase is “high surface area to volume ratio” — examiners expect to see this linked to why properties change at the nanoscale. In “evaluate” questions about nanoparticles, always cover both benefits and risks to access the top marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Transition metals are harder, denser, and have higher melting points than Group 1 metals. They also form coloured compounds and act as catalysts (e.g. iron in the Haber process).
  • Nanoparticles (1–100 nm) have a very high surface area to volume ratio, which gives them different properties from the same material in bulk — used in sunscreens, catalysts, medicine, and electronics.
  • The long-term health and environmental effects of nanoparticles are not yet fully understood — the exam expects you to evaluate both the benefits and the risks.
