lessons.title: Yield, Atom Economy, Molar Concentrations and Gas Volumes
lessons.description: Calculating percentage yield, atom economy, molar concentrations and gas volumes at RTP.
lessons.content_html:
Percentage Yield

In any chemical reaction, the amount of product you actually make is almost always less than the amount you expected. The theoretical yield is the maximum mass of product calculated from the balanced equation, but the actual yield is whatever you collect at the end of the experiment.

To compare the two, chemists calculate the percentage yield using this equation:

Key Fact

Percentage yield = (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100

A percentage yield of 100% would mean you collected every gram of product the equation predicted. In practice this never happens because:

  • The reaction may be reversible, so not all reactants convert to products.
  • Some product is always lost during transfer — for example, liquid left behind on glassware or solid stuck to filter paper.
  • Unexpected side reactions may form different products from those intended.

A student expected to produce 495 tonnes of product A but only obtained 400 tonnes. Calculate the percentage yield.

Percentage yield = (400 ÷ 495) × 100 = 80.8%

Atom Economy

atom economy measures how much of the total mass of reactants ends up as the useful product. It is a way of judging how wasteful a reaction is before you even carry it out.

Key Fact

Atom economy = (Mr of desired product ÷ total Mr of all products) × 100

A high atom economy means most atoms from the reactants end up in the useful product, generating less waste. Industries prefer reactions with high atom economy because they are more sustainable and more cost-effective.

Calculate the atom economy for making hydrogen by reacting zinc with hydrochloric acid:

Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2

Mr of desired product (H2) = 2. Total Mr of all products = ZnCl2 (136) + H2 (2) = 138.

Atom economy = (2 ÷ 138) × 100 = 1.4%

This extremely low atom economy shows that this method wastes almost all the reactant mass as zinc chloride — an unwanted by-product.

Reactions that produce only one product, such as addition reactions, have an atom economy of 100%. Reactions that produce several products, where only one is useful, have a low atom economy.

Molar Concentrations

You already know that concentration can be measured in g/dm³. For more advanced calculations, chemists express concentration in \(mol/dm^{3}\) (moles per cubic decimetre). This tells you how many moles of solute are dissolved in each dm³ of solution.

Key Fact

Concentration (mol/dm³) = moles of solute ÷ volume of solution (dm³)

To convert between units, remember: 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³. So if a volume is given in cm³, divide by 1000 to get dm³.

A student dissolves 0.5 mol of sodium hydroxide in 250 cm³ of water. Calculate the concentration in mol/dm³.

Volume in dm³ = 250 ÷ 1000 = 0.25 dm³

Concentration = 0.5 ÷ 0.25 = \(2 mol/dm^{3}\)

You can also rearrange the equation to find moles or volume:

  • Moles = concentration × volume (in dm³)
  • Volume (dm³) = moles ÷ concentration

Molar Volume of Gases

Equal numbers of moles of any gas occupy the same volume at the same temperature and pressure. At room temperature and pressure (RTP), the molar volume of any gas is \(24 dm^{3}\) (or 24,000 cm³).

Key Fact

Volume of gas (dm³) = moles × 24. This works for any gas at RTP — hydrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide or any other.

You can rearrange to find moles from a volume: moles = volume (dm³) ÷ 24.

Calculate the volume of 7 moles of oxygen gas at RTP.

Volume = 7 × 24 = \(168 dm^{3}\)

You can combine gas volume calculations with reacting mass problems. First use the balanced equation to find the moles of gas produced, then multiply by 24 to get the volume at RTP.

For example, if a reaction produces 0.5 mol of CO2, the volume at RTP is 0.5 × 24 = \(12 dm^{3}\).

Yield vs Atom Economy — What’s the Difference?

percentage yield tells you how efficiently the reaction was carried out in practice — it compares what you actually got to what you should have got. atom economy tells you how efficient the reaction itself is by design — whether the equation produces waste products or not.

A reaction can have a high atom economy but a low percentage yield (if the method was poorly carried out), or a low atom economy but a high percentage yield (if you collected nearly all the useful product, but the reaction still creates lots of waste).
lessons.exam_tip_html: In calculation questions, always show your working clearly — you can earn method marks even if your final answer is wrong. For atom economy, make sure you divide by the Mr of all products, not all reactants. For gas volume questions, check whether the volume is given in cm³ or dm³ before using 24 or 24,000. Label every answer with the correct unit.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Percentage yield compares actual yield to theoretical yield — it is always less than 100% because of losses, reversibility, or side reactions.
  • Atom economy compares the Mr of the desired product to the total Mr of all products — higher is more sustainable.
  • Concentration in mol/dm³ = moles ÷ volume (dm³). One mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³ at RTP.

lessons.title: Titrations, Chemical Cells and Fuel Cells
lessons.description: Acid-alkali titrations, chemical cells and batteries, and hydrogen fuel cells.
lessons.content_html:
Titrations

A titration is a technique used to find the precise concentration of an acid or alkali. It works by reacting an acid with an alkali of known concentration and measuring the exact volume needed to achieve neutralisation. This is one of the most important required practicals in GCSE Chemistry.

Titration Equipment

A titration uses specialised glassware to achieve accurate results. A burette is a long graduated tube with a tap at the bottom, used to deliver the acid in a controlled way. A pipette is used to measure a precise, fixed volume of the alkali — typically 25.0 cm³. The alkali is placed in a conical flask on a white tile so colour changes are easy to see.

Key Fact

A burette measures the volume of acid added. A pipette measures the fixed volume of alkali. An indicator shows when neutralisation is complete.

Carrying Out a Titration

Follow these steps to carry out an acid–alkali titration:

1. Use the pipette to add exactly 25.0 cm³ of alkali (e.g. sodium hydroxide) into a clean conical flask. 2. Add 2–3 drops of a suitable indicator, such as phenolphthalein (pink in alkali, colourless in acid). 3. Fill the burette with acid of unknown concentration. Record the initial burette reading. 4. Perform a rough titration first: add the acid 1 cm³ at a time whilst swirling the flask, until the indicator changes colour. This gives an approximate volume. 5. Record the final burette reading and calculate the titre (final − initial reading). 6. Repeat, but this time add the acid quickly until you are about 5 cm³ below your rough titre, then add it dropwise until the colour change occurs. 7. Repeat until you obtain at least two concordant results — results within 0.10 cm³ of each other.

The end point is the exact moment the indicator permanently changes colour — for phenolphthalein, this is when the solution goes from pink to colourless. The mean of the concordant results gives the accurate titre, which is used in calculations. The rough titre is always excluded from the mean.

Key Fact

Concordant results are within 0.10 cm³ of each other. Calculate the mean of the concordant results only — always discard the rough titre.

Titration Calculations

Once you have the accurate titre, you can calculate the unknown concentration using the formula:

M₁V₁ = M₂V₂

Where M₁ is the concentration of the alkali, V₁ is the volume of the alkali, M₂ is the concentration of the acid, and V₂ is the mean titre (volume of acid). If three values are known, you can rearrange to find the fourth. For example, if 20.0 cm³ of 0.10 mol/dm³ NaOH is neutralised by 13.3 cm³ of HCl, the concentration of HCl = (0.10 × 20.0) ÷ 13.3 = 0.15 mol/dm³.

Chemical Cells and Batteries

A chemical cell produces electricity from a chemical reaction. When two different metals are placed into an electrolyte (an electrically conducting liquid) and connected by a wire, the more reactive metal loses electrons more readily. These electrons flow through the wire to the less reactive metal, creating an electric current.

The voltage (potential difference) produced by a chemical cell depends on: the types of metals used as electrodes — the greater the difference in reactivity between the two metals, the higher the voltage; and the electrolyte used. For example, a cell with magnesium and copper electrodes will produce a higher voltage than one with zinc and copper, because magnesium is much more reactive than zinc. A battery is simply two or more cells connected in series.

In non-rechargeable cells, the chemical reactions are irreversible — once the reactants are used up, the cell stops working. In rechargeable batteries, the reactions can be reversed by connecting to an external power supply, allowing the battery to be used again. Alkaline batteries (like AA batteries) are non-rechargeable, while lithium-ion batteries in phones and laptops are rechargeable.

Hydrogen Fuel Cells

A hydrogen fuel cell is an electrochemical device that generates electricity by combining hydrogen and oxygen. Unlike a battery, it does not run out — as long as hydrogen and oxygen are supplied, it keeps producing electricity.

Hydrogen gas enters at the anode (negative electrode) and is oxidised, losing electrons. These electrons flow through an external circuit to the cathode (positive electrode), creating a current. At the cathode, oxygen reacts with the electrons and hydrogen ions to form water. The overall reaction is: hydrogen + oxygen → water (2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O). The only waste product is water, making fuel cells very clean.

Higher tier: At the anode, the half equation is 2H₂ → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻. At the cathode, the half equation is O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O.

Key Fact

The only waste product from a hydrogen fuel cell is water. This makes them much cleaner than fossil fuel engines, which produce carbon dioxide and other pollutants.

Advantages of hydrogen fuel cells: the only waste product is water (no CO₂); they do not run out as long as fuel is supplied; and they are more efficient than combustion engines. Disadvantages: hydrogen is difficult and expensive to store and transport safely (it is highly flammable); producing hydrogen itself often requires energy from fossil fuels (unless from electrolysis using renewable energy); the infrastructure for hydrogen refuelling is limited; and fuel cells are currently expensive to manufacture.

By contrast, rechargeable batteries can be charged from the mains (convenient), but they eventually degrade and need replacing; their production uses finite resources (lithium, cobalt); and charging from fossil-fuel electricity still produces emissions indirectly.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Titration questions often ask you to describe the method in a set order — practise writing out the steps without prompts. For “Explain” questions on chemical cells, always link the reactivity difference between the metals to the voltage produced. Fuel cell questions frequently ask you to “compare” or “evaluate” — make sure you give both advantages and disadvantages with clear scientific reasoning, not just a list.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A titration uses a burette, pipette, and indicator to find the exact volume of acid needed to neutralise an alkali. Concordant results (within 0.10 cm³) are averaged to give the accurate titre.
  • Chemical cells produce electricity when two different metals in an electrolyte are connected — the greater the reactivity difference, the higher the voltage. A battery is two or more cells joined together.
  • Hydrogen fuel cells produce electricity from hydrogen and oxygen with water as the only waste product, but storing hydrogen safely and building infrastructure remain challenges.
